headline: Working group agreed to raise inclusionary zoning threshold to 13 units and voted to remove Cambrian Rise from Waterfront District rules
summary: The Planning Commission and City Council Ordinance Committee working group discussed seven proposed amendments to ZA-27-01 Inclusionary Zoning with invited housing experts and the public. The group reached a compromise to raise the IZ unit threshold to 13 units, and took informal votes on waterfront district tiering, including removing Cambrian Rise from the Waterfront District. The Planning Commission adopted its minutes and accepted communications.
decisions: The working group took an informal vote and removed Cambrian Rise from the Waterfront District requirements, 6-2, with E. Mahnke and E. Malone voting against.
The working group voted on the waterfront requirement percentage, 5-3, with G. Bergman, E. Mahnke, and E. Malone voting against.
The group reached a compromise to raise the IZ project threshold to 13 units, between the staff-recommended 17 units and the 10 units some panelists proposed.
The Planning Commission adopted the minutes and accepted communications by unanimous vote.

5. Welcome & Introductions with Invited Panelists 
6. Staff Presentation of proposed Amendment ZA-27-01 Inclusionary Zoning 
The meeting focused on discussing seven inclusionary zoning amendment proposals as part of 
Burlington's broader housing strategy. Staff presented the proposals, including raising the project 
threshold from 5 to 17 units, eliminating tiering requirements, allowing offsite units anywhere, and 
reconfiguring payment-in-lieu calculations. 
7. Discussion related to Proposed Amendment ZA-27-01 with IZ Experts
Collaborative Working Group on Inclusionary 
Zoning Meeting Minutes – 7/14/26 
p. 2 
  
   
 
The meeting focused on discussing affordable housing policies and development thresholds in 
Burlington. Bushor recommended lowering the development threshold from 17 to a lower number 
like 13 units to encourage more smaller-scale housing developments, particularly for 
homeownership opportunities. The panelists agreed that removing tiering requirements and 
allowing off-site development options would help increase affordable housing production, with 
particular support for using payment-in-lieu funds to support both large-scale developments and 
smaller conversion projects like turning rental properties into homeownership units . The discussion 
highlighted the need to balance affordable housing requirements with market feasibility, especially 
for smaller developers entering the market, while ensuring adequate funding flows into the Housing 
Trust Fund to support various affordable housing initiatives. 
8. Discussion related to ZA-27-01 Proposals 1 & 2 amongst Working Group 
Proposal 1, IZ Threshold: The group discussed the inclusionary zoning (IZ) threshold for housing 
developments, with staff recommending 17 units while offering 13 as a midpoint option.  The 
discussion focused on balancing the trade-offs between maintaining IZ requirements and 
encouraging overall housing production, with staff noting that increasing the threshold might result 
in fewer IZ units but could potentially be offset by other housing creation tools like development 
agreements and public-private partnerships. Ultimately, the group reached a compromise on raising 
the threshold to 13 units as a middle ground between the staff-recommended 17 units and the 10 
units proposed by some panelists. 
Proposal 2, IZ Tiering: The group discussed but did not reach a consensus on waterfront district 
tiering, with debate between maintaining 25% requirements versus reducing them to 20%, and 
whether to remove Cambrian Rise from waterfront district requirements . The Working Group 
conducted an informal vote, which resulted in Cambrian Rise being pulled out of the Waterfront 
District (6-2, E. Mahnke and E. Malone voted against) and reducing the waterfront requirement from 
20% to 20% (5-3, G. Bergman, E. Mahnke, and E. Malone voted against).  
9. Public Forum related to ZA-27-01 
Sharon Bushor: IZ is an affordability tool, not the tool to help us get to 7,000 units but will help make 
sure that some of those will be affordable for low- and moderate-income people. 
Was a commitment that she understood the value system of Burlington. Its an 
equity an inclusion tool but will not help with neighborhood code with RL and RM  
because those have a maximum of 8 units per parcel. Supports going to 10, not 13. 
Its about the people, not the units. As far as the tiering system, looks to the experts 
and agrees with the 2 Tier. Because of equity, thinks the waterfront needs to be 
25%. If it went to 20%, it would at least be something. Try not to disincentive with 
Payment in Lieu.  
Evan Gould: Generally okay with compromise at 13 units. Because the Working Group was 
comparing Burlington’s proposed policies to Portland, OR, wanted to point out that, 
per state statute in Oregon, they cannot do unsubsidized IZ. Every IZ unit in Portland 
requires a subsidy and is not paid for by the developer.  Minneapolis is the same 
way, and most projects there are subsidized IZ. With the Waterfront tiering, his 
observation is that most of the development of large units in the Waterfront 
happened in old RL-W zones that no longer exist and there haven’t been that many 
large projects in those districts, and wonders how much the very large tiering has 
affected that. Census block groups that have become “More Inclusionary” are not 
the ones located on the waterfront. How many actual IZ units were created in the 
old Waterfront districts?
Collaborative Working Group on Inclusionary 
Zoning Meeting Minutes – 7/14/26 
p. 3 
  
   
 
Todd DeLuca: Has looked a lot at IZ as a policy, feels it’s a failed policy in Burlington. Would like to 
see it repealed. Supports proposals on the table. Central problem is that it targets 
developers as the funders. Doesn’t want less housing development in Burlington, but 
we’ve been placing heavy burdens on developers. In a 2017 evaluation showed that 
development rate dropped after IZ was adopted and that few IZ units have been 
created. In terms of getting low-income housing into the buildings, there are plenty 
of examples where that isn’t the case. 2017 study also says that most IZ projects 
were not in high income neighborhoods and thinks that IZ integration has failed. 
Funded or subsidized affordable housing is more effective. Thinks that affordable 
housing trust fund using short term rental taxes is more effective.
